items.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I saw the connection between Stan Kenton, Woody Herman, and Tito Puente, and Machito.

ctx.x: Okay. We have jazz the way we know it, the swing stuff, the bebop, which I wanted to be a jazz drummer at first before I ever got into the Latin thing. So in college I was into Mel Lewis, you know, Buddy Rich of course, Stan Kenton. I went to North Texas State University. So I was studying and playing in the lab. I’ve always loved straight ahead jazz you know and of course I used to listen to all the bebop stuff, Miles Davis and all that stuff. But then one day somebody in the dorm heard me playing some Mexican…

blew my mind away because of the rhythm. It was so strong. And then I started to hear like the bands of Machito, who did a lot of what we call now Latin jazz for me it’s the marriage of both because for instance in straight ahead Latino, like a dance tune, it might have one chord like we did yesterday. It might have a 1-4-5 progression [scats] or a 2-5- 1 or a 1-6-2-5. You know, the basic chord structure, and of course jazz — it still has that but it might have so many other chords, especially like a ballad. So…

Okay. Good answer. Your band mates speak of this music with great reverence for its history and lineage and yesterday’s lecture-demonstration was a lot about spirituality. But the music exists in the spiritual realm as well as the secular realm. It is — what might happen — I’ll rephrase. Would there be something that a person could do with this music that would be irreverent and frowned upon? If you’re playing music that’s connected with spirituality and deities, can it be abused?
